_comment: Curated measure→issue mappings for the Voting Record 'stance vs. record' verdict. Applied by applyCuratedIssueSeed() in netlify/lib/vr-ingest.ts. Each entry attaches to EVERY real measure with the same (congress, chamber, canonical number) that already exists — created by the seed migration or by a live Congress.gov ingest. measureType is recorded for provenance but is deliberately NOT part of the match: a live ingest that files H.Res. 1399 as a 'bill' must still receive the curated mapping, and a number that exists twice must have both rows mapped rather than one silently missed. Entries that don't match anything yet are harmless no-ops until that roll call is ingested, so nothing here can invent a measure. supportMeaning is binary: 'yea_supports' (a yea advances the issue) or 'yea_opposes' (a yea cuts against it) — see _voteEffectiveSupport in stance-helpers.js.

issues.rationale: Extends and expands the 2017 individual and business tax cuts.
Enacts net spending reductions through budget reconciliation.
Reduces federal Medicaid spending and tightens eligibility; a yea vote cuts against expanding healthcare access.
Provides new funding for border enforcement and immigration operations.
Expands onshore and offshore oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal land.
Mandates detention and removal proceedings for covered unauthorized immigrants.
Tightens immigration enforcement.

Section 2 of the bill as passed the House adds a new INA 236(c)(1)(E) requiring the Secretary of Homeland Security to detain an inadmissible alien charged with, arrested for, convicted of, or who admits having committed burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting, and to issue a detainer and take custody. A yea attaches a mandatory custodial consequence to those offences. Weighted 55, identical to S. 5's mapping, so the two Laken Riley vehicles score the same axis at the same strength. Note the House bill reaches ONLY those four property offences: assault of a law enforcement officer and crimes resulting in death or serious bodily injury entered the statute later, through the Senate's S.Amdt. 14 and S.Amdt. 8.

Section 3, 'Enforcement by attorney general of a State', amends INA 235(b) (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)) to give the attorney general of a State, or another authorised State officer, standing to sue the Secretary of Homeland Security in federal district court over alleged violations of the detention and removal requirements that harm the State or its residents. A yea creates a state cause of action against the federal government. Weighted 40, identical to S. 5's mapping. The same section is what the Senate's S.Amdt. 23 tried and failed to strike. Re-keyed from states_federal_power in the August 2026 taxonomy split: a cause of action against the federal government now has its own key.

measures._comment: The bill that actually became Public Law 119-1. H.R. 29 above is the House's own Laken Riley bill, which passed the House on 2025-01-07 and went no further; the Senate took up its own S. 5, amended it, and both chambers passed that. Senate roll 119/1/7 and House roll 119/1/23 are votes on S. 5, not on H.R. 29 — see migration 20260804000000_vr_repair_laken_riley_measure_identity.sql. These four mappings are carried from H.R. 29 because the curated rationale still describes S. 5's text; the values below are byte-identical to the ones that migration inserts, because applyCuratedIssueSeed() upserts with onConflictDoUpdate and would otherwise overwrite them on the next POST /seed-issues.

issues.rationale: Mandates detention and removal proceedings for covered unauthorized immigrants.
Tightens immigration enforcement.
Triggered by arrest for burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in death or serious bodily injury.
issues._comment: Restated from the CRS summary of Public Law 119-1 rather than copied from H.R. 29. H.R. 29's rationale enumerates the House bill's narrower trigger list; S. 5 as enacted adds larceny and the death/serious-bodily-injury clause via the Senate amendment (roll 119/1/6, Ernst, agreed 75-24). Reusing the H.R. 29 sentence here would have understated the enacted text.

issues.rationale: Gives state attorneys general standing to sue the federal government over certain immigration-detention and enforcement decisions; a yea expands state authority to contest federal enforcement choices in court. Re-keyed from states_federal_power in the August 2026 taxonomy split: a cause of action against the federal government now has its own key.
SAVE Act — requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
Adds a citizenship-documentation requirement to voter registration.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections. A yea adds a documentary precondition to federal voter registration.

Requires documentary proof of United States citizenship — a passport, a REAL ID showing citizenship, or a birth certificate presented with photo ID — before a state may register an applicant for a federal election, requires states to run a removal program against federal databases for non-citizens already on the rolls, and creates criminal penalties for officials who register an applicant without the documentation. Eligibility verification is the core of the safeguard facet, so a yea is a vote for tighter verification. Not marked primary only because election_integrity already holds that flag on this measure from an earlier pass and moving it would change a published mapping rather than add one.
Sets the fiscal blueprint and reconciliation instructions that framed the year's tax-and-spending changes.
Directs committees to find net spending reductions through reconciliation.
Reserves reconciliation room to extend and expand the 2017 tax cuts.
Congressional Review Act resolution repealing the IRS reporting rule for decentralized-finance brokers; a yea rolls back the mandate.

Nullifies the IRS rule that extended broker tax-reporting duties to decentralized-finance platforms, so those platforms are not required to collect and report user transaction data. A yea removes that reporting duty from decentralized software. Enacted as Public Law 119-5.
Reasserts congressional authority over tariffs by ending the emergency used to impose them; a yea rolls back the executive tariff action.
Removes the duties on Canadian imports; a yea favors lower trade barriers with a top trading partner.
Terminates the national emergency declaration that is the legal basis for the tariffs on Canadian imports; a yea ends those duties. Passed the Senate 51-48 and did not advance in the House.
Requires congressional authorization before military action against Iran; a yea favors restraint and a congressional check on war-making.

A privileged joint resolution under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution directing removal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran absent congressional authorization; a yea asserts that the authorization decision belongs to Congress. Re-keyed from america_first_fp in the August 2026 taxonomy split, which narrowed that key to foreign aid and open-ended commitments; who authorizes the use of force now has its own key. Weight 70 preserved. The resolution's controlling axis is still the posture toward the conflict, which the restraint row carries at 100.

Requires congressional authorization before continued U.S. hostilities against Iran and directs the removal of forces from hostilities Congress has not authorized. A yea withdraws U.S. forces from an ongoing engagement absent a vote of Congress.
Exempts qualified tip income from federal income tax for tipped workers.
Aims to raise take-home pay for service and hospitality workers.
Reduces the federal tax burden on a category of earned income.
Repeals the waiver behind California's EV sales mandate; a yea rolls back a major state climate rule.

Revokes the Clean Air Act waiver behind California's Advanced Clean Cars II rule, ending the requirement that a rising share of new vehicles sold be zero-emission in California and in the dozen states that adopted it. A yea keeps internal-combustion vehicles saleable in those markets.
Uses the Congressional Review Act to strike a federal waiver/rule.
Repeals the waiver behind California's zero-emission truck mandate; a yea rolls back a major state climate rule.

Revokes the Clean Air Act waiver behind California's Advanced Clean Trucks rule, ending the requirement that a rising share of new medium- and heavy-duty truck sales be zero-emission. A yea removes that limit on conventional truck sales.
Uses the Congressional Review Act to strike a federal waiver/rule.

Authorizes FY2026 appropriations for Department of Defense military activities, military construction, and Department of Energy defense activities (the NDAA); a yea funds and authorizes the armed forces.
Amendment (to H.R. 3944) to limit disclosures regarding earmarks; a yea reduces disclosure, cutting against transparency and anti-corruption.

Homeowner Energy Freedom Act repeals the DOE high-efficiency electric home rebate program, state home-energy contractor training grants and building energy code adoption assistance (IRA/P.L. 117-169); a yea rolls back federal climate/electrification programs.
The bill also rescinds unobligated balances for the rebate and building-energy-code programs, so a yea cancels appropriated federal spending.

Information Quality Assurance Act requires agencies to publish the critical factual material relied on in rulemaking and guidance, and to use the best reasonably available evidence; a yea expands disclosure of the government's factual basis.

Norman amendment to H.R. 3838 (FY2026 NDAA) prohibits providing gender transition procedures, including surgery or medication, through the Exceptional Family Member Program; a yea bars transgender care for military dependents.

Biggs amendment to H.R. 3838 (FY2026 NDAA) would bar designating military and certain National Guard lands as Endangered Species Act critical habitat and exempt military operations from ESA prohibitions; a yea reduces habitat protection on federal land.

Stop Insider Trading Act amends chapter 131 of title 5 to bar Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependents from holding or trading covered individual stocks; a yea is a direct vote for the congressional stock-trading ban.

Secondary: the bill's enforcement machinery is disclosure-based — advance public notice of covered transactions and published divestiture certifications — so a yea also expands financial-disclosure transparency. Weighted below the primary because the bill is not a general transparency measure.

FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act — authorizes DoD military activities, military construction, DOE defense activities, and personnel strengths; a yea funds and authorizes the armed forces. Weighted 80 rather than 100 because this NDAA also carries unrelated social-policy riders (see H.Amdt. 254-256), so passage is not a pure defense-posture signal.

Title XII, Subtitle C is headed "Matters relating to Israel": Sec. 1221 extends the war reserve stockpile authority for Israel, Sec. 1222 extends United States-Israel anti-tunnel and subterranean warfare cooperation, and Sec. 1223 extends cooperation on countering unmanned aerial systems. Sec. 219 establishes a United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative. A yea enacts all four and keeps U.S. security aid and joint weapons development flowing; a nay blocks the bill that carries them. Weighted 40 for share of the vehicle: this is a subtitle plus one section inside a defense authorization, not the bill's purpose.

Protecting Privacy in Purchases Act bars payment-card networks from requiring or assigning a merchant category code that singles out firearms retailers; a yea blocks a gun-purchase tracking mechanism that gun-rights groups oppose.
Take Care of America's Veterans Act amends titles 10 and 38 to improve veterans' benefits and VA administration; a yea expands veterans' benefits.
21st Century ROAD to Housing Act is a housing-supply package — it targets the regulatory and financing barriers to new residential construction; a yea is a vote to build more housing.
Secondary: the same package also carries affordability and federal housing-assistance provisions, so a yea advances housing affordability generally, not only new supply.

Jayapal War Powers concurrent resolution directing the President under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran; a yea ends US participation in an undeclared conflict.

Tlaib War Powers concurrent resolution directing the President under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon; a yea ends US participation in an undeclared conflict.

Boebert amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) would codify Executive Order 14183, requiring all personnel to serve in accordance with their biological sex and thereby banning transgender service members; a yea removes an existing protection for transgender people.

Mace amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) prohibits gender-related medical care under TRICARE and bars TRICARE from covering gender-related procedures and treatments; a yea withdraws transgender health coverage.

Mace amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) prohibits male participation in female sports at Department of Defense Education Activity schools — a transgender sports-participation ban for military-dependent students; a yea restricts transgender participation.

McDowell amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) would authorize the Secretary of Defense to establish a school choice pilot program for members of the Armed Forces; a yea creates a publicly funded school-choice program.

Crank amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) establishes a presumption of approval for DoD servicemembers and civilian employees seeking their commander's authorization to carry personal firearms on military installations; a yea expands lawful carry.

Fine amendment to H.R. 8595 (FY2027 national security and State appropriations) would strike the $139,575,000 appropriation for the Global Environment Facility, the main US multilateral climate- and environment-finance channel; a yea defunds international climate finance. Weighted 75 because it is a single line item rather than a change in domestic climate policy.

Self amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) codifies protections and responsibilities for military chaplains and makes violations of those protections punishable under the Uniform Code of Military Justice; a yea strengthens statutory religious-exercise protection in the services.
Amends the Federal banking laws to widen small-business and Main Street access to capital; a yea backs that expansion of access.

Lessens and modifies Federal banking regulation as its operative purpose: new banks get a three-year phase-in to meet certain capital requirements, certain rural community banks get a reduced leverage ratio, financial regulators must tailor regulatory actions to an institution's risk profile and business model and review their regulations more often and more widely, and higher asset thresholds exempt more financial companies and banks from various fees and reporting requirements while letting more small banks qualify for a longer examination cycle. A yea enacts that relief.

Eases the competition review that bank mergers currently pass through: it allows financial regulators to approve certain bank mergers without considering whether the merger is noncompetitive or monopolistic, and raises the asset threshold above which a financial holding company needs Federal Reserve Board approval to acquire a company, so more acquisitions close without that approval. A yea removes those checks.
Directs the Committee on Ethics to preserve and publicly release records of monetary settlements involving sexual harassment; a yea forces disclosure of settlements that are otherwise sealed.

Amends title II of the Social Security Act to reauthorize demonstration authority for the disability insurance program; a yea keeps that Social Security program authority in place. Weighted below a full-strength mapping on purpose: this is program administration, not a vote on benefit levels.
Prohibits funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel — a direct floor test of whether to continue a standing foreign-aid commitment.
The amendment reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by the corresponding amount; a yea cuts that spending.

Prohibits funds appropriated by the FY2026 National Security and State Department appropriations Act from being used for Israel and reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3.3 billion accordingly — a direct floor attempt to zero out U.S. security assistance to Israel. Failed 104-314 with 10 members voting present. A yea ends the assistance.
Prohibits funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Jordan — a direct floor test of whether to continue a standing foreign-aid commitment.
The amendment reduces the National Security Investment Programs and Foreign Military Financing accounts by the corresponding amounts; a yea cuts that spending.
Ensures the continued operation of the Santa Ynez production unit; a yea keeps a domestic oil production asset online rather than letting it shut down.
The amendment's stated purpose is protecting a critical component of the military's fuel supply chain; a yea backs that supply-chain security.

Establishes a small business regulatory budget, capping the regulatory cost federal agencies may impose; a yea constrains new regulation. Identified from the H.Res. 916 rule already in this record, which describes H.R. 2965 as the small business regulatory budget bill.
The regulatory budget is scoped to the compliance burden borne by small businesses; a yea reduces that burden.

Creates an SBA hotline for small businesses to report federal rules they find burdensome; a yea backs that channel. Identified from the H.Res. 916 rule already in this record, which describes H.R. 4305 as the SBA Red Tape Hotline bill.
The hotline exists to surface federal red tape for repeal or revision; a yea advances that deregulatory review.
A Congressional Review Act resolution whose entire operative effect is to nullify a federal rule; a yea strikes the CFPB overdraft regulation off the books.

The nullified rule required very large financial institutions to cap overdraft charges at $5, justify a higher cap, or treat overdrafts as credit subject to Truth in Lending Act disclosure; a yea removes that constraint on what the largest banks may charge.

Removes Endangered Species Act protection from the San Francisco Bay-Delta longfin smelt by nullifying its listing; a yea strips a federal conservation protection. Mapped to the conservation key because the vocabulary has no dedicated wildlife or endangered-species key.
A Congressional Review Act resolution striking a federal agency rule; a yea removes the Fish and Wildlife Service regulation.
Requires public elementary and secondary schools to disclose funds received from, or contracts with, a foreign source; a yea compels disclosure that is currently not required.

Requires schools to notify parents of their right to request and receive information about foreign influence in their child's school; a yea creates a parental notification right that does not exist today.
Establishes a disclosure-on-request regime for foreign influence in schools as a condition of federal education funding; a yea widens what schools must reveal.

The FY2027 congressional budget resolution. Its published CRS summary states that it 'provides reconciliation instructions for legislation that increases the deficit', directing four House committees to report legislation increasing the deficit over FY2027-FY2036 by not more than specified amounts; a yea adopts a fiscal blueprint whose reconciliation instructions authorise deficit increases. Direction read off the summary, the mirror of the deficit-reducing instructions that set the direction on H.Con.Res. 14.

The KIDS Act requires online platforms to adopt age-identification technology on sites where a third of the content is sexual material harmful to minors, to default minors' social-media accounts to settings that limit compulsive-usage features and adult contact, to give parents account and privacy controls, and to make AI chatbots disclose their nature to minors; a yea imposes those guardrails. Mapped to the key whose own vocabulary is age verification, social media, AI and guardrails.

Amendment to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA) striking section 521 and replacing it with a prohibition on foreign nationals attending the United States Military Academies, which ends a U.S.-funded training relationship with the officer corps of partner nations; a yea restricts the academies to Americans.

Cadet places for partner-nation officers are one of the working mechanisms of long-run allied military relationships; a yea removes them, cutting against leading through allied commitments. Same framing as the H.Amdt. 251 mapping already in the record.

Part A amendment No. 1 to H.R. 8800 (FY2027 NDAA), offered by Rep. Boebert as designee for the author, Rep. Roy: 'Strike section 1213 (and redesignate accordingly).' Section 1213 amends the FY2022 NDAA to move the Afghanistan War Commission's final-report deadline from 3 years to 4, so striking it keeps the 3-year deadline and a yea insists the commission's public report arrive on the schedule Congress originally set. Weighted below a full mapping because it changes when a report is delivered, not what must be disclosed.

Part A amendment No. 44 to H.R. 8800 (Harrigan) adds 10 U.S.C. 2661(e): no federal funds may purchase, install, operate, maintain or contract for an automated speed enforcement camera system on a military installation, and any system already in operation must be decommissioned and removed within 180 days. A yea removes an automated camera-surveillance enforcement system and takes down the ones already running. Weighted low on purpose: the prohibition reaches military installations only, and the amendment expressly preserves cameras used for security, access control, force protection and criminal investigation — so it is not a vote on surveillance policy generally.

Part A amendment No. 316 to H.R. 8800 (Grothman) requires the Secretary of Defense to report within 180 days on options for reducing the number of civilians employed by the Department by 200,000, including an assessment of current non-uniformed personnel levels and recommendations for achieving the reduction while maintaining readiness. A yea asks for a plan to shrink the civilian workforce. Weighted low on purpose: the amendment commissions a report, it does not reduce anything.

The report must include 'an analysis of the anticipated cost savings associated with such reductions', so the amendment puts a 200,000-position federal payroll reduction on the table as a savings measure and a yea backs studying it. Secondary and low-weight for the same reason as the primary — this is a reporting requirement, not a cut.

Part A amendment No. 15 to H.R. 3838 (Mace, Tenney) inserts a new section barring the Superintendent of a Service Academy from allowing a cadet or midshipman who is male to participate in any athletic program or activity designated exclusively for females, with 'male' and 'female' defined by reproductive biology; a yea restricts transgender participation. Same instrument and same direction as H.Amdt. 255 (Mace, DoDEA schools) and H.Amdt. 85 (Norman, EFMP care), both already mapped at full weight. Purpose text taken from the Rules Committee report accompanying H.Res. 682, because no source we previously held carried it — see migration 20260727000000, which created this measure row deliberately without a mapping.

Title IX expands the child tax credit to $3,000 per child ($3,600 under age six), makes it fully refundable and advanceable, and provides the $1,400-per-person recovery rebates. Direct household support for families is the largest single line of the act.
Recovery rebates, expanded earned income and child tax credits, and emergency rental and utility assistance are all directed at household costs during the pandemic.
Title IX subtitle F expands Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for 2021 and 2022, removing the 400%-of-poverty eligibility cliff and subsidising COBRA continuation coverage.

The act was enacted through budget reconciliation as unoffset emergency spending; a yea adds to the deficit rather than reducing it. Weighted below the primary because the fiscal effect is a consequence of the relief, not its stated purpose.
Title II provides child care stabilization funding, supplemental Child Care and Development Block Grant appropriations, and Head Start funding.
Title II establishes the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund for reopening and learning-loss mitigation, the largest federal appropriation to K-12 schools in the period.
Title IX extends pandemic unemployment compensation programs and exempts a portion of 2020 unemployment benefits from income tax.
Title V funds the Restaurant Revitalization Fund, additional Paycheck Protection Program and Economic Injury Disaster Loan support, and the Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program.
The act's opening paragraph enumerates roads, bridges, ports, airports, the electric grid and water systems as its subject; surface transportation reauthorization is Division A.
Division B reauthorizes federal public transportation programs and Division C funds passenger and freight rail, including the largest Amtrak investment since its creation.
Division F establishes the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program and the Affordable Connectivity Program to extend service to unserved and underserved areas.
Division E funds drinking water and wastewater infrastructure, lead service line replacement, and Western water infrastructure including storage and drought resilience.
Division D and Division J fund coastal resiliency, wildfire risk reduction, and grid hardening against extreme weather.

The act funds clean school buses, electric vehicle charging networks, weatherization, and legacy pollution remediation. Weighted as a secondary because these are components of an infrastructure package rather than its organising purpose.
The act's new spending was only partially offset; a yea increases the deficit. Weighted low for the same reason as the climate slice — it is a consequence, not the stated purpose.
Division A funds domestic semiconductor fabrication and Division B authorises the federal science agencies' research and innovation programs. Semiconductor competitiveness is the act's named subject.
Sec. 103 expands financial assistance to incentivise investment in U.S. facilities and equipment for semiconductor production, including a dedicated program for mature technology nodes.

Sec. 102 establishes the CHIPS for America Defense Fund for the National Network for Microelectronics Research and Development, and the International Technology Security and Innovation Fund for secure semiconductor supply chains.
The act appropriates new unoffset funding for the CHIPS funds; a yea increases the deficit.

Subtitle D, Part 1 modifies and extends the production and investment tax credits for wind, solar, geothermal, biomass and hydropower, and the act's energy security title is its largest spending component.

Sec. 11001 requires CMS to negotiate maximum prices for high-spend brand-name Medicare drugs beginning in 2026, scaling from 10 drugs to 20 by 2029. The act also caps insulin cost sharing and Medicare Part D out-of-pocket spending.
Sec. 12001 extends through 2025 the expanded premium tax credit, including eligibility for taxpayers above 400% of the federal poverty line.
Sec. 10101 imposes a 15% minimum tax on the adjusted financial statement income of corporations above $1 billion, and Sec. 10201 a 1% excise tax on publicly traded corporations' stock buybacks.

The same two sections are, on their face, corporate tax increases. Mapping both directions is deliberate: a corporate minimum tax is simultaneously an accountability measure and a tax increase, and the record should show both rather than pick the flattering one.

Part 6 raises offshore royalty rates but also directs Interior to accept the highest bid for Gulf of Mexico Lease Sale 257 and to hold Lease Sales 258, 259 and 261, and Sec. 50265 conditions new wind and solar rights-of-way on holding oil and gas lease sales.

Title I, Subtitle A is captioned "Deficit Reduction" and contains the corporate minimum tax, the buyback excise tax and IRS enforcement funding. Weighted low because the act's net fiscal effect is contested, but the subtitle heading and its contents are what the enacted text says.

Title II requires enhanced background check review for purchasers under 21, creates federal straw purchasing and trafficking offenses, and closes the dating-partner gap in the domestic violence prohibitor.

Division A, Title I is a children and family mental health title: CCBHC demonstration extension, pediatric mental health care access grants, and Medicaid telehealth and school-based services guidance.
The same Title II provisions restrict firearms acquisition for 18-to-20-year-old purchasers and extend a possession prohibitor to a new class of persons; a yea narrows firearms access.
The act funds school safety programs and school-based mental health service capacity, including Medicaid guidance directed specifically at services delivered in schools.
The entire act expands VA eligibility, presumptions of service connection and benefits for toxic-exposed veterans. Named subject, no ambiguity.
The mechanism is an expansion of VA health care enrolment and treatment eligibility, not only cash benefits.

The act repeals DOMA's man/woman definitions and requires interstate recognition of same-sex marriages. Mapped as a single key deliberately: a religious_liberty contradiction row would be false, because the enacted text expressly states it does not affect religious liberties and does not require religious organizations to provide goods or services for a marriage.

The act's purpose is to stabilise a universal public service: it removes the prepayment obligation that drove reported Postal Service losses, integrates postal retiree health coverage with Medicare, and requires six-day delivery.
The act requires the Postal Service to publish an online public dashboard of service-performance data by delivery unit.

Annual defense authorization: end strengths, procurement, military construction and DOE national security programs. No national_debt row, because the BILLSTATUS summary lists programs without a topline figure and asserting one would be unsourced — the same reason H.R. 3838 carries a debt slice (its summary cites a topline) and this one does not.

Sec. 1669 makes available not more than $108,000,000 to the Government of Israel to procure Iron Dome components through co-production in the United States, not more than $30,000,000 for David's Sling Weapon System co-production on a one-for-one cash match, and not more than $62,000,000 for the Arrow 3 Upper Tier Interceptor Program — $200,000,000 of missile-defense co-production in one section. Sec. 1551 establishes a Department of Homeland Security United States-Israel cybersecurity grant program and authorizes not less than $6,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026. Sec. 1316 establishes the Cyprus, Greece, Israel and United States 3+1 Interparliamentary Group. A yea funds and continues that backing. Weighted 35 for share of the vehicle: the enacted act also carries the Department of State Authorization Act of 2021 and a division of non-Defense matters.

Sec. 6610, the Blocking Deadly Fentanyl Imports Act, amends section 481(e) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (22 U.S.C. 2291(e)) to add a majors-list category for a country that is a significant source of illicit synthetic opioids significantly affecting the United States, and amends 22 U.S.C. 2291h(a) with a new paragraph (10) requiring the International Narcotics Control Strategy Report to identify the most significant source countries for illicit fentanyl and describe how far each is cooperating. A yea enacts that listing authority and that reporting duty. Weighted 25, the floor of this record: one section working through a designation criterion and a report, against the four-section BUST Fentanyl Act subtitle that carries the same key on S. 1071 at 40.

Annual defense authorization. Mapped on the enacted content only; the sole House roll BILLSTATUS attaches to this vehicle (roll 253/2022) is the suspension vote on the rivers-and-harbors bill the NDAA text later replaced, so no House margin is claimed for it.

Division C, Title III is a permitting-reform title: it narrows the scope of National Environmental Policy Act administrative review, sets page and time limits on environmental reviews, and designates a lead agency. A yea speeds federal project review. Re-keyed from gov_regulation in the August 2026 taxonomy split — the row was always about how long a federal review takes, not about the size of the federal rulebook. Weight 70 and primary status preserved: the NEPA title is what this mapping was always reading.
Sec. 324 ratifies every existing federal authorization for the Mountain Valley Pipeline, directs the issuance of any remaining ones, and removes them from judicial review.

Division C tightens Temporary Assistance for Needy Families work requirements and raises the SNAP able-bodied-adults-without-dependents work-requirement age to 54 while reducing the discretionary exemption pool from 12% to 8%. A yea narrows safety-net eligibility, notwithstanding the new exemptions for homeless individuals, veterans and former foster youth.
Division B terminates the suspension of federal student loan payments and resumes interest accrual, and bars the Secretary from extending it further absent new statutory authority.

Annual defense authorization. A yea authorizes the fiscal year 2024 defense topline and the personnel, procurement, research, military-construction and Department of Energy national-security programs under it.

Section 7902 of the enacted act reauthorizes Title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978, the authority under which section 702 collection against targets outside the United States runs, through April 19, 2024. A yea extends that authority. Weighted as a provision-level slice rather than as the bill's headline: this is one section of a whole defense authorization.
Annual defense authorization with an added servicemember quality-of-life title covering pay, housing and family support.

Sec. 708 bars TRICARE from covering treatment for gender dysphoria that could result in sterilization for dependents under 18. This is the provision behind the vote's party inversion — Clerk roll 500/2024 split Republican 200-16 in favour and Democratic 81-124 against, the only NDAA in this window a majority of one party opposed.

The act extends warrantless section 702 collection for two years and broadens the electronic communications service provider definition. Held at 85 rather than 100 because the same act repeals "abouts" collection authority, imposes supervisory and attorney approval for U.S.-person queries, bars political appointees from sensitive-query approval, adds penalties and requires 180-day audits — the direction is a net extension of surveillance authority, but calling it unmixed would misstate the text.
The act preserves a foreign intelligence collection authority the intelligence community identifies as a core counterterrorism and counterintelligence tool; a yea sustains it.
Divisions A, B and C are security assistance appropriations for Israel, Ukraine and the Indo-Pacific respectively. A yea funds alliance commitments across three theatres.

The package is the largest single foreign-aid appropriation of the 118th Congress, and Division B is Ukraine security assistance specifically. A yea is a vote against the position that resources should be redirected from foreign aid to domestic priorities.
The same three security-assistance divisions deepen U.S. involvement in two active conflicts and one deterrence posture; a yea is a vote against military restraint.

Division D carries the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, requiring divestiture of foreign-adversary-controlled applications or prohibiting their distribution in the United States.

Division E is the Fentanyl Eradication and Narcotics Deterrence Off Fentanyl Act: sanctions in response to the national emergency relating to fentanyl trafficking, plus anti-money-laundering measures against the transnational organizations involved.

measures._note: Division B of H.R. 815 as a standalone bill. The House never voted the H.R. 815 package — it passed four division bills on 2024-04-20 and H.Res. 1160 combined them into the Senate amendment. Only this one divided the chamber (311-112, Republicans 101-112 against their own majority), so it is the House-side record of the Ukraine substance. Its keys are a strict subset of the parent's: no tech_balance and no immig_fentanyl, because the TikTok divestiture and the fentanyl sanctions are in Divisions D and E, which this bill does not contain.

For the People Act of 2021. Title I requires every state to offer automatic voter registration through motor-vehicle and other designated agencies, same-day registration and online registration, and restricts voter-roll purges; Title II requires at least fifteen consecutive days of early voting and no-excuse absentee voting with prepaid return postage, and restores voting rights to citizens released from incarceration. Every one of those provisions widens a registration or casting pathway, so a yea is a vote to expand access. The bill's election-security title is deliberately NOT mapped: it mandates durable paper ballots and risk-limiting audits while the same bill permits a sworn statement in lieu of documentary ID and restricts list maintenance, so one yea covers both directions of the safeguard facet and records neither.

John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2021. Restores the Voting Rights Act preclearance regime with a rolling twenty-five-year coverage formula and adds a practice-based review list that gates specific access-narrowing changes — new documentary or photo-ID requirements, polling-place closures and consolidations, and voter-roll purges — behind federal review before they take effect, and restores a private right of action. The bill adds no verification requirement, ballot-handling rule or audit provision of its own, so it is mapped to the access facet only; mapping it to election_security would score members on a question the text does not ask.

Freedom to Vote: John R. Lewis Act, moved as a House amendment to the Senate amendment to H.R. 5746 — a shell bill whose Clerk vote description still reads 'NASA Enhanced Use Leasing Extension Act of 2021', so the roll is identified by citation and question rather than title. Requires automatic and same-day registration, a minimum of two weeks of early voting including weekends, no-excuse mail voting with ballot tracking and a minimum number of drop boxes per jurisdiction, and makes Election Day a public holiday. A yea is a vote to expand access. Its election-security title is not mapped, for the same internal-split reason as H.R. 1, whose text it incorporates.

Same text as H.R. 884 in the 119th Congress: amends the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to bar non-citizens from voting in District elections. A yea is a vote for citizenship verification as a condition of voting. Same Home Rule Act confound — a nay may be a home-rule position rather than a position on non-citizen voting — and it is recorded here for the same reason.
Removes a casting pathway created by District law; a yea narrows who may cast a ballot. Same Home Rule Act confound as above.

SAVE Act, 118th Congress. Amends the National Voter Registration Act to require documentary proof of United States citizenship before a state may register an applicant for a federal election, requires states to establish a program to identify and remove non-citizens from existing rolls using federal immigration and Social Security databases, and creates criminal penalties for officials who register an applicant without the documentation. Eligibility verification and roll maintenance are both squarely in the safeguard facet, so a yea is a vote for tighter verification.

The documentary requirement must be satisfied in person at a registration office, which as a practical matter closes registration by mail and online to any applicant who cannot present documents there, and the acceptable-document list does not accommodate a citizen whose current legal name differs from the name on their birth certificate. The bill adds a barrier at the registration step, so a yea is a vote against easier registration. This is the opposite direction from the same measure's election_security row on purpose: the two facets are scored independently and this bill genuinely pulls them apart.

Amends the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to bar any individual who is not a United States citizen from voting in a District election, repealing the effect of the Local Resident Voting Rights Amendment Act of 2022. Citizenship as a condition of casting a ballot is an eligibility safeguard, so a yea is a vote for tighter verification of who may vote. Confound recorded rather than hidden: because the vehicle amends the Home Rule Act, a nay may express opposition to Congress overriding a local District enactment rather than support for non-citizen voting. The mapping is made on the operative election provision and no member's reason is inferred from the vote.

Removes an existing casting pathway: non-citizen District residents who registered under the 2022 local law lose the ability to vote in municipal elections. A yea narrows who may cast a ballot. Same Home Rule Act confound as the election_security row above.

SAVE America Act, the text the House substituted into S. 1383 on 2026-02-11 and passed 218-213 on roll 69. Mapped on the substitute's own provisions, read from the engrossed House amendment: a state "shall not accept and process an application to register to vote in an election for Federal office unless the applicant presents documentary proof" of citizenship under any registration method; a new HAVA section bars an official from providing a ballot to an in-person voter who does not present "a valid physical photo identification" and requires mail voters to enclose a copy or the last four Social Security digits with an affidavit; states must submit their full voter lists to the Department of Homeland Security for comparison against the SAVE system and remove non-citizens on verified information; and new criminal penalties reach an official who registers an applicant without the documentation. Verification at registration, identification at casting, roll maintenance and fraud enforcement are the four things this facet covers, and the substitute does all four in the same direction, so a yea is a vote for tighter safeguards. The Clerk's record for roll 69 still shows the Senate short title "Veterans Accessibility Advisory Committee Act" because S. 1383 was the vehicle; the substituted text is what the House voted on and what this mapping is made from.

The substitute adds a barrier at both steps this facet measures. At registration, a mail-form applicant must present proof "in person to the office of the appropriate election official" by the registration deadline, which closes mail and online registration to anyone who cannot appear; at casting, photo identification becomes a precondition for receiving an in-person ballot, and an in-person voter without one may only cast a provisional ballot and must cure it within three days. The bill's easing provisions were read and weighed rather than ignored: an alternative-evidence pathway on a perjury attestation, a required process for applicants whose documents carry a former name, free public access to a copier or scanner in government buildings, and exemptions for uniformed-services and certain elderly and disabled voters. Each of those accommodates the new requirement rather than widening access on its own, so the yea does not point both ways here and the facet is not declined the way it is on H.R. 1 and H.R. 5746. Weighted above H.R. 8281's 70 because that bill reached only the registration step while this one also conditions casting.

Bipartisan Background Checks Act of 2021, passed 227-203 on 2021-03-11. Section 3 adds a new subsection (aa) to 18 U.S.C. 922 making it unlawful for an unlicensed person to transfer a firearm to another unlicensed person unless a licensed importer, manufacturer or dealer first takes possession, runs the 922(t) background check as if the firearm came from its own inventory, and records the transfer. Background-check screening is the first thing this facet covers, and the bill extends it to the private-sale channel that 922(t) does not currently reach, so a yea tightens screening. Exceptions for close-family gifts, transfers by operation of law, temporary transfers to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm, and temporary transfers while hunting or at a range narrow the reach of the requirement but not its direction.

The same section conditions an otherwise-lawful transfer between two eligible private parties on a licensed dealer's involvement and a recorded transaction, which is a licensing and record burden on the acquisition step this facet protects — the reason the bill was opposed as a step toward a transfer registry. Weighted 55 and not higher because the operative text changes nothing else the facet measures: no new prohibited category of person or firearm, no category ban, and no restriction on carrying. A person eligible to acquire a firearm before the bill is eligible after it; only the channel changes.

Enhanced Background Checks Act of 2021, passed 219-210 on 2021-03-11. Replaces the three-business-day default-proceed period in 18 U.S.C. 922(t)(1)(B)(ii) — the window after which a dealer may complete a sale on a check that has returned no answer — with a minimum of ten business days, after which the prospective purchaser may petition for expedited review that gives the system a further ten days before the transfer may proceed. A yea gives an incomplete background check time to complete, which is the screening instrument this facet measures. The companion to H.R. 8 and voted the same day; H.R. 8 extends the check to a new channel, this bill strengthens the check itself, and the two are mapped separately because a member could and some did split them.

Protecting Our Kids Act, passed 223-204 on 2022-06-08 — the House's own six-title answer to Uvalde and Buffalo, and the broadest firearms package either chamber passed in the window. Every operative title is this facet in the tightening direction: Title I bars a licensed dealer from selling a semiautomatic centerfire rifle or shotgun that accepts a detachable magazine to anyone under 21; Title II creates federal straw-purchase and trafficking offences with penalties and forfeiture; Title III defines a ghost gun and brings assembling, molding, machining or 3D-printing a frame or receiver within "manufacturing firearms", with carve-outs for permanently inoperable firearms, those serialized under state law within thirty months and pre-1968 firearms; Title IV adds Ethan's Law, a new 18 U.S.C. 922(z)(4) offence for storing a firearm in a residence where the person knows or reasonably should know a minor is likely to gain access without permission or a resident is ineligible, with an express exception where the firearm is carried on or within immediate control of the person; Title V adds a bump stock to 26 U.S.C. 5845(a)(9); Title VI adds a new 18 U.S.C. 922(v) banning large-capacity ammunition feeding devices with a grandfather for devices lawfully possessed on or before enactment. Screening, trafficking enforcement and safe storage are three of the four things this facet covers and the bill does all three.

Three of the six operative titles remove firearms or configurations from lawful acquisition or possession by an eligible adult: Title I bars 18-to-20-year-olds from an entire class of long gun, Title V reclassifies a bump stock under the National Firearms Act, and Title VI bans large-capacity magazines outright going forward. Title III's extension of serialization to a self-made frame or receiver is a further condition on lawful acquisition. Weighted 80 rather than 100 because that is provision arithmetic and not a hedge: Title II (trafficking and straw purchases) and Title IV (safe storage) take nothing away from an eligible adult — trafficking was already unlawful conduct and the storage offence carries an express exception for a firearm kept on or within immediate control, so neither reaches the scope of the right. The bill's six title-retention roll calls (117-2 rolls 237 through 242) are the best provision-level evidence in the window and are deliberately NOT ingested, because a curated mapping attaches to a measure and every roll of that measure would inherit this composite direction; only the passage roll is ingested.

Federal Extreme Risk Protection Order Act of 2021, passed 224-202 on 2022-06-09. Creates a new 18 U.S.C. 932 authorising a United States district court to bar a named person from possessing, receiving, shipping or transporting a firearm or ammunition, on petition by a family or household member or a law-enforcement officer, where the court finds the person poses a significant danger of causing personal injury to self or others; provides an ex parte track with a prompt follow-on hearing, requires surrender to a designated law-enforcement officer, and penalises a knowingly false petition. Red-flag and extreme-risk removal is named in this facet's scope, and this is the only federal extreme-risk bill either chamber voted in the window, so a yea is the cleanest available record on that instrument.

Assault Weapons Ban of 2022, passed 217-213 on 2022-07-29 — the first House passage of an assault-weapons ban since 1994. Bans the import, sale, manufacture, transfer and possession of a "semiautomatic assault weapon", defined by a one-feature test: a semiautomatic rifle able to accept a detachable magazine plus any one of a pistol grip, a forward grip, a folding, telescoping or detachable stock, a barrel shroud or a threaded barrel, with parallel definitions for pistols and shotguns and an enumerated model list. Assault-style restriction is named in this facet's scope; the bill is that instrument and nothing else, which is why the mapping is weight 100 with no other safety provision to slice.

The clearest opposite-direction reading of either facet in this pass: a broad category ban on commonly-owned firearms is the exact instrument this facet's scope note names as the thing gun_rights support opposes, and a yea narrows what an eligible adult may lawfully acquire or keep. Weighted 95 rather than 100 only because the ban grandfathers firearms lawfully possessed on the date of enactment and exempts law enforcement and the armed forces, so it does not reach what a current owner already holds; the secure-storage condition on transferring a grandfathered firearm is the one place it does touch existing possession.

Congressional Review Act joint resolution disapproving ATF final rule 2021R-08F, "Factoring Criteria for Firearms with Attached 'Stabilizing Braces'". Passed the House 219-210 on 2023-06-13 and was DEFEATED in the Senate 49-50 on 2023-06-22, so this pass carries a recorded vote from both chambers on one measure. The rule reclassified a large share of braced pistols as short-barreled rifles subject to National Firearms Act registration and taxation, requiring owners to register, permanently alter or surrender a configuration they lawfully held. Voiding it removes a registration and tax-stamp obligation from a lawful configuration and, under 5 U.S.C. 801(b)(2), bars a substantially similar rule without new statutory authority — Second Amendment protection against registry and licensing burdens is named in this facet's scope, so a yea is a vote for the right as this facet defines it.

The rule the resolution voids is a screening-and-registration instrument: it brought a configuration into the National Firearms Act's registration, background-check and transfer-tax regime, and disapproval removes it and forecloses a substantially similar rule. That is this facet in the loosening direction, so a yea is scored as opposition here. Weighted 70 rather than matching the rights side, because the resolution changes no statute this facet measures — no background-check requirement, no removal process, no storage rule and no trafficking provision is touched. What it reaches is one agency's classification of one accessory, and the Congressional Review Act's all-or-nothing form gives a member no way to vote on the regime while rejecting the rule.

Kennedy amendment to the Military Construction, Veterans Affairs appropriations division of H.R. 4366, agreed to 53-45 on 2023-10-25 with eleven Democrats voting yea, and ENACTED as Section 413 of Division A of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 (P.L. 118-42, 138 Stat. 65). The enacted text bars using Division A funds to report to the Attorney General, for National Instant Criminal Background Check System purposes, that a person deemed mentally incapacitated, mentally incompetent or experiencing an extended loss of consciousness has been adjudicated a mental defective under 18 U.S.C. 922(d)(4) and (g)(4), unless a judicial authority has found the person is a danger to themselves or others. A yea restores the eligibility of veterans who were prohibited by an administrative fiduciary determination rather than a judicial finding, which is the scope of the right this facet measures. Mapped at 100 because the amendment does this one thing; it is also the only recorded vote in the window on a firearms provision that became law apart from S. 2938, which is why an amendment roll is admitted here at all. Its vehicle H.R. 4366 is deliberately left UNMAPPED: a vote on a multi-division appropriations act is not a firearms position.

The provision removes a class of record from the background-check system, so a yea loosens the screening instrument this facet measures. Weighted 75 rather than 100 because the removal is narrow and conditional in a way the headline is not: it reaches only Veterans Affairs fiduciary determinations under 38 U.S.C. 5502, leaves every other mental-health prohibitor and reporting channel intact, and preserves reporting where a judicial authority has found the person dangerous. As enacted it also ran only for the fiscal year the division funded — H.R. 1041 in the 119th is the attempt to make the same policy permanent law, which is why the two are mapped as a matched pair.

Veterans 2nd Amendment Protection Act, passed 216-201 on 2026-05-21. Adds a new 38 U.S.C. 5501B barring the Department of Veterans Affairs from transmitting a beneficiary's personally identifiable information to the Department of Justice for inclusion in the National Instant Criminal Background Check System on the basis of a 38 U.S.C. 5502 determination that the beneficiary cannot manage their own benefit payments and requires a fiduciary, unless a judge, magistrate or other judicial authority has found the beneficiary is a danger to themselves or others. A yea restores the eligibility of veterans prohibited by an administrative determination rather than a judicial finding. The permanent-law version of S.Amdt. 1354, which imposed the same policy for one fiscal year as an appropriations restriction; mapped identically so the pair is comparable across chambers and Congresses.

Removes a class of record from the background-check system permanently rather than for one fiscal year, so a yea loosens the screening instrument this facet measures. Weighted 75 for the same reason as its appropriations predecessor: the change reaches only Veterans Affairs fiduciary determinations, leaves every other mental-health prohibitor and reporting channel intact, and preserves reporting where a judicial authority has found the person dangerous.

issues.rationale: Amendment to S. 5 (Laken Riley Act) whose stated purpose is 'To expand the list of criminal offenses that subject inadmissible aliens to mandatory detention.' A yea widens the set of people the Secretary of Homeland Security must take into custody and place in removal proceedings. Agreed to 70-25 and carried into Public Law 119-1, so this is enacted text and not a message vote.

The operative change is to the LIST OF CRIMINAL OFFENCES that triggers the detention mandate, so a yea attaches a mandatory custodial consequence to a broader set of crimes. Weighted above S. 5's own tough_on_crime mapping (55) rather than below it: the bill does many things and this amendment does only this one, so the crime-severity axis is a larger share of what a senator was voting on.

measures._comment: Ernst amendment to S. 5 (Laken Riley Act), agreed to AS AMENDED by S.Amdt. 14, 75-24 on 2025-01-20, roll call 119/1/6 — minutes before the Senate passed S. 5 64-35 on roll 119/1/7. Its text is in Public Law 119-1. This is the amendment that the descriptive measure row 'Senate Amendment to S. 5' was standing in for; that row carries no roll call and this one does.

issues.rationale: Amendment to S. 5 (Laken Riley Act) whose stated purpose is 'To include crimes resulting in death or serious bodily injury to the list of offenses that, if committed by an inadmissible alien, require mandatory detention.' A yea widens the set of people the Secretary of Homeland Security must take into custody and place in removal proceedings. Agreed to 75-24 and carried into Public Law 119-1.

The offences this amendment adds are defined by their RESULT — death or serious bodily injury — rather than by category, so it is the most direct crime-severity test in the bill's whole floor consideration. H.R. 29 as passed the House and S. 5 as introduced reached only burglary, theft, larceny and shoplifting; this is where the death-or-serious-injury trigger enters the statute. A yea attaches mandatory detention to the gravest offences on the list.

This is the record's only roll call isolating that provision from the rest of the bill, which is what makes it worth a measure row of its own.

issues.rationale: Amendment to S. 5 (Laken Riley Act) whose stated purpose is 'To strike the section that authorizes State attorneys general to sue Federal immigration authorities for alleged violations relating to the detention of aliens.' A YEA REMOVES a state cause of action against the federal government, so a yea cuts against letting states take Washington to court — the mirror of S. 5's own mapping, which is yea_supports because passing the bill is what created the standing. Rejected 46-49, so the section survived into Public Law 119-1. Re-keyed from states_federal_power in the August 2026 taxonomy split. Weight 100 and primary status preserved: this is the record's only roll call isolating the provision.

measures._comment: Epstein Files Transparency Act, Public Law 119-38 (signed 2025-11-19). One recorded vote in the entire legislative history: house 119/1/289, under suspension of the rules, 427-1 with 5 not voting. The Senate passed it the next day without amendment by unanimous consent, so no Senate roll exists to find. A 427-1 roll confirms a stated transparency position but distinguishes almost nobody — the sponsorship record (Khanna as sponsor, Massie as original cosponsor, four months before the floor caught up) is the part of this history that differentiates, and it is written to vr_positions rather than being forced into a second issue mapping here.

issues.rationale: Requires the Department of Justice to publish, in a searchable and downloadable format, all unclassified records relating to the investigation and prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein — including materials relating to Ghislaine Maxwell, flight logs and travel records, and the individuals named or referenced, government officials among them — and to report to Congress within 15 days the categories released and withheld, a summary of redactions, and a list of the government officials and politically exposed individuals named. A yea compels disclosure the executive branch had withheld. This is the whole substance of the Act: it creates no offence and changes no penalty, so gov_transparency carries it alone.

measures._comment: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Public Law 119-60 (signed 2025-12-18). Easy to mis-identify three ways. S. 1071 was introduced 2025-03-14 as a bill to disinter the remains of Fernando V. Cota from Fort Sam Houston National Cemetery and passed the Senate by unanimous consent; the House struck the entire text, substituted the NDAA, and passed it 312-112 (house 119/1/320), after which the Senate agreed to the House amendment 77-20 (senate 119/1/648). The Clerk's vote-desc for House rolls 319 and 320 STILL PRINTS the disinterment title, so nothing here may be written from the roll-call page's description. S. 2296 (the Senate's own FY2026 NDAA, passed 77-20 on 2025-10-09) and H.R. 3838 (the House vehicle) are not the enacted law, and the H.R. 8800 already in the record is the FY2027 NDAA. Cornyn sponsored the shell vehicle and is NOT the NDAA's author. 'S. 1071' matches more than one row in vr_measures, so the migration applies this mapping to every row with that number. Four axes are mapped and five are declined with reasons — see declinedFacets in db/vr-landmark-vote-seed.json. The israel_support axis was declined in that pass and mapped by 20260911000000 once runbook rule 22's "section inside a vehicle" bar was retired; the old refusal is preserved in reversedFacets.

issues.rationale: The annual defence authorisation: Divisions A through H authorise Department of Defense military activities, military construction, Department of Energy national security programs, personnel strengths and the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026. A yea authorises and equips the armed forces. Weighted 80 rather than 100 for the same reason as the FY2027 NDAA (H.R. 8800): the enacted text folds in fourteen separately titled Acts, several unrelated to defence posture, so passage is not a pure defence-posture signal.

Division H, Title LXXXIII, Subtitle B (Secs. 8311-8314) is the Break Up Suspicious Transactions of Fentanyl Act — the BUST Fentanyl Act — enacted through this vehicle: it amends the Fentanyl Sanctions Act, adds fentanyl-trafficking reporting to the International Narcotics Control Strategy Report, and requires a study and report on fentanyl trafficking originating in the People's Republic of China. A yea enacts new sanctions authority and reporting aimed at fentanyl traffickers. Weighted 40 on purpose: it is one named subtitle inside an omnibus, and it works through sanctions and reporting rather than a direct enforcement change.

Section 512 inserts a new 32 U.S.C. 328a: the chief executive of a State that has declared an emergency due to a disaster may order a member of that State's National Guard who is serving on Active Guard and Reserve duty to perform State disaster-response duty. A yea hands a governor direct authority over federally paid Guard personnel. Weighted 25 — the lowest mapping in that pass — because the authority is gated on the Secretary of Defense's consent, is reimbursable by the State, and is capped at 14 days per member per calendar year (extendable by 7 days, or by 46 for a catastrophic incident). It is a real Title 32 shift toward the states, but it is one narrow section of a 312-112 defence authorisation and must not be read as a referendum on who commands the Guard. Re-keyed from states_federal_power in the August 2026 taxonomy split.

Six provisions of the enacted text back Israel militarily. Sec. 864 establishes a United States-Israel Defense Industrial Base Working Group. Title XII, Subtitle D is headed "Matters Relating to Israel": Sec. 1231 extends and modifies anti-tunnel cooperation, Sec. 1232 extends and modifies cooperation to counter unmanned systems in all warfighting domains, and Sec. 1235 requires a report on joint United States-Israel military exercises. Sec. 1657 makes available not more than $60,000,000 to the Government of Israel for Iron Dome components, $40,000,000 for the David's Sling Weapon System and $100,000,000 for the Arrow 3 Upper Tier Interceptor Program, each through co-production in the United States. Sec. 1706 requires a continual assessment of the impact of international state arms embargoes on Israel. A yea enacts all of it. Weighted 35 rather than the FY2027 NDAA's 40 because this text folds in fourteen separately titled Acts across eight divisions, so the same subtitle is a smaller share of what was voted on.

measures._comment: Secure America Act, Public Law 119-98 (signed 2026-06-10). A reconciliation bill under title II of S. Con. Res. 33 appropriating $69.545 billion to the Department of Homeland Security for FY2026, passed 52-47 in the Senate (roll 119/2/163) and 214-212 in the House (roll 119/2/214). Four axes are mapped and six are declined with reasons — see declinedFacets in db/vr-secure-america-vote-seed.json. The mapping is written from the ENROLLED TEXT, and the distinction that text forces is why tough_on_crime appears at all: every Title I appropriation (Secs. 101, 102, 103(a)(6)) is expressly limited to functions OTHER than immigration enforcement and customs functions, because Title I is the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee's reconciliation jurisdiction and cannot reach immigration enforcement, while Title II is the Judiciary Committee's and says in terms that its money is for immigration enforcement. Reading the bill off its short title would collapse that split and score all $69.5B as one undifferentiated enforcement vote. Note also that the axes are attached to the MEASURE and therefore apply at full strength to both passage rolls, which is the reason each weight below is argued from a dollar share rather than assigned by feel.

issues.rationale: Title II is the largest part of the Act and is interior immigration enforcement in terms: Sec. 201 appropriates $13.020 billion to CBP "in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities", and Sec. 202 appropriates $31.075 billion to ICE across nine purposes that name removal directly — transportation costs "associated with alien departure or removal operations" (2), information technology, facility and fleet sustainment each "to support enforcement and removal operations" (3)-(5), and attorneys in the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor "to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings" (7). Paragraph (9) sets aside not less than $350,000,000 for detainer management, custodial transfer and arrests of covered unlawful aliens, and (9)(C) forbids those funds from being used to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention or otherwise facilitate the release into the community of anyone encountered. A yea funds removal operations at $44.095 billion, 63 percent of the Act. Primary at 100: this is what the bill is.

Sec. 101 appropriates $9.550 billion to hire, pay, train and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel; Sec. 103 appropriates $3.450 billion for nonintrusive inspection equipment at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern and maritime borders, Air and Marine platforms for rapid response, border surveillance technology upgrades, and the biometric entry and exit system under 8 U.S.C. 1365b; and Secs. 104 and 203 add $5.000 billion for the purposes of their respective titles. A yea funds border personnel and border technology at $26.020 billion counting Sec. 201's CBP hiring. Weighted 90 rather than 100 only because deportations carries the larger share and is the primary; this is far more border-specific than the Laken Riley Act's border_security mapping (70), which rested on a detention mandate rather than on any border appropriation.

Two of Sec. 103(a)'s six enumerated purposes are narcotics interdiction, and the statute names the drug: paragraph (1) funds new nonintrusive inspection equipment "including artificial intelligence, machine learning, and other innovative technologies … to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders", and paragraph (5) funds "[e]nhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals" at those same borders. A yea funds interdiction capability aimed at fentanyl and its precursors. Weighted 50: above the FY2026 NDAA's immig_fentanyl mapping (40), because that one worked through sanctions and reporting while this is direct detection and interdiction money, and well below the enforcement axes, because Sec. 103 is $3.450 billion — 5 percent of the Act — and fentanyl is two of its six purposes.

Sec. 102 appropriates $7.450 billion to hire, pay, train and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel, and closes with an express carve-out: "funds provided in this section shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions." That makes it, by the statute's own terms, $7.450 billion of federal CRIMINAL investigation capacity rather than immigration money, and it earmarks $108,500,000 of it for additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts at the Victim Identification Laboratory of the Child Exploitation Investigations Unit and at the Special Agent in Charge offices, plus training of State and local law enforcement, "to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse", within the HSI Cyber Crimes Center. A yea funds investigators for those crimes. Weighted 40 and not higher: Sec. 102 is 10.7 percent of the Act, the members who voted no did so on the enforcement titles rather than on this section, and it adds investigative staffing rather than changing any offence or sentence. The related criminal-alien definitions in Sec. 202(9)(D) are deliberately NOT counted here — they are already carried by deportations, and counting them twice would inflate this axis.

measures._comment: Cortez Masto amendment to S.Amdt. 5453 to S. 2 (Secure America Act), REJECTED 45-53 on 2026-06-05, roll call 119/2/160. One key, because the amendment does one thing. It is in the record because it splits the chamber the opposite way from passage: the 52-47 and 214-212 party-line passage rolls make S. 2 a near-perfect party proxy, and this roll asks the same senators a different question — whether to fund local police hiring out of the same bill — and gets a different answer. tough_on_crime is declined for it; see declinedFacets in db/vr-secure-america-vote-seed.json.

issues.rationale: The amendment's stated purpose is its entire substance: "To appropriate amounts for local law enforcement hiring programs." A yea adds funding for State and local police staffing to a bill whose $69.545 billion otherwise goes entirely to federal Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement; a nay leaves it out. back_police is the chip "Fund police and impose tougher penalties for violent crime", and this amendment is the funding half of it in isolation — no offence, penalty or sentence is touched. Primary at 100 because a single-purpose amendment has no second axis. Rejected, so no local hiring line is in Public Law 119-98.

measures._comment: Gallego amendment to S.Amdt. 5453 to S. 2 (Secure America Act), REJECTED 47-52 on 2026-06-05, roll call 119/2/156. The record's only roll call isolating DACA from the enforcement bill it was offered to, and the only one in this pass that tests the immigration axis in the pathways direction rather than the enforcement direction. deportations is declined for it on the same reasoning that kept S.Amdt. 23 (Coons) off that key in the previous pass — see declinedFacets in db/vr-secure-america-vote-seed.json.

issues.rationale: The amendment's stated purpose is its entire substance: "To make funds available for the timely adjudication of DACA renewal applications." A yea funds processing of renewals under the existing Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals policy, whose recipients lose work authorisation and protection from removal when a renewal lapses in the backlog; a nay leaves the bill's $69.545 billion entirely with border and immigration enforcement. immigration_reform is the chip "Create earned pathways to citizenship for long-settled immigrants" and its keyword set names DACA and Dreamers directly. Primary at 100 because a single-purpose amendment has no second axis, with one honest qualification recorded here: the amendment funds ADJUDICATION of an existing deferred-action policy and creates no pathway of its own, so it tests support for protecting long-settled DACA recipients rather than support for a new status. Rejected 47-52, so no renewal-adjudication funding is in Public Law 119-98.

measures._comment: Rescissions Act of 2025, Public Law 119-28 (signed 2025-07-24) — the first rescission request under section 1012 of the Impoundment Control Act to be enacted since 1999. THIS ENTRY IS NOT THE WHOLE MAPPING. The measure carries SEVEN live rows in vr_measure_issues: cut_spending, gov_waste and national_debt from migration 20260719150000_seed_rescissions_voting_record.sql, and america_first 60, audit_spending 55, gov_services 45 yea_opposes and free_speech 30 yea_opposes from 20260721140000_seed_legislation_deepdive.sql. The first three are mirrored below byte-identically on purpose, because applyCuratedIssueSeed() upserts with onConflictDoUpdate and any drift here would silently overwrite the live rationale; only their measure-level sourceUrl is new (the 20260719150000 rows carry no source_url). The four from 20260721140000 are deliberately NOT mirrored and are left exactly as that pass wrote them — omitting a key from this file changes nothing about the live row, because the upsert only touches the keys the seed carries. america_first_fp is the one genuinely NEW mapping this pass adds, and it sits beside the already-live america_first: same substance, but america_first_fp is the chip whose text names foreign aid and the chip 22 rostered members hold a stance on, against 4 for america_first. Both are yea_supports, so they cannot contradict; the opposite-direction precedent is H.R. 815 (118th), mapped america_first_fp 70 yea_opposes by 20260810000000. NOT ADDED, and recorded so the reasoning is visible: foreign_balance ('lead through NATO and allied diplomacy') — two members can read the same yea in opposite directions there, and it is the general-posture chip the alignment-tool.js Israel comment warns against loading with specific votes; checks_balances — the direction of a congressional rescission of a presidential impoundment request is not stable (a yea both ratifies the President's proposal and exercises Congress's own power of the purse), and 20 rostered members hold stances on that key, so a wrong direction would be expensive. gov_services is a disagreement rather than a decline: this pass would not have mapped a public-broadcasting rescission to a Social-Security-and-Medicaid chip, but reversing another pass's published judgement needs its own migration and its own argument, not a silent omission.

issues.rationale: Rescinds previously appropriated funds, cutting federal spending.

Cancels roughly $9 billion in budget authority Congress had already enacted, rescinding it from foreign-assistance accounts and from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. A yea returns appropriated money to the Treasury unspent.
Modestly reduces outlays against the federal deficit.

Nineteen of the enrolled Act's twenty rescission paragraphs strike unobligated foreign-assistance balances, roughly $7.9 billion in all: Development Assistance $2.5B, Economic Support Fund $1.65B, Migration and Refugee Assistance $800M, International Disaster Assistance $496M, Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia $460M, International Organizations and Programs $436.9M, Global Health Programs $500M, the Clean Technology Fund $125M, USAID Operating Expenses $125M and the United States Institute of Peace $15M, among others. The america_first_fp chip reads "Put U.S. interests first, end endless wars and rethink foreign aid commitments" — rescinding appropriated foreign aid is that chip's own stated content, so a yea supports it. Weighted 65 and not primary because the measure's controlling axis is still spending, not foreign policy.

measures._comment: HALT Fentanyl Act, Public Law 119-26 — permanently places fentanyl-related substances in schedule I. All three mappings below are MIRRORS of rows already live in vr_measure_issues, first written by migration 20260721170000_seed_legislation_expansion.sql; weight, isPrimary, supportMeaning and rationale text are reproduced byte-identically because applyCuratedIssueSeed() upserts and drift would overwrite live values. Mirrored here so this pass's two roll calls (senate 119/1/127 and the House's 321-104 passage at house 119/1/166) satisfy the seed-discipline gate, which requires every measure a roll call attaches to be mapped in this file. No new keys added: the existing three already state the axes honestly, including health_mental as yea_opposes for the treatment-and-research objection raised on the floor.

issues.rationale: Directly targets the fentanyl overdose crisis by making class-wide Schedule I placement of fentanyl-related substances permanent.
Attaches mandatory-minimum penalties and quantity triggers to fentanyl-analogue offenses.

Permanently places fentanyl-related substances as a class in Schedule I and applies to them the quantity thresholds and mandatory-minimum prison terms that attach to fentanyl analogues, while adding a registration pathway for Schedule I research. A yea sets the federal response to this class of substances in criminal-penalty terms.

measures._comment: Stop Illegal Entry Act of 2025 — a two-section sentencing bill amending INA sections 275 and 276, passed the House 226-197 on 2025-09-11 (roll 119/1/264) and received in the Senate with no further action. NOT law. New measure in this pass; both mappings are new, and both are written from the engrossed text (BILLS-119hr3486eh) rather than a secondary description. DECLINED for this measure: deportations ('deport people here illegally') — the bill changes the sentence imposed AFTER a criminal conviction, and expands no removal authority, no detention capacity and no expedited-removal ground, so a yea is not a vote to remove more people; immigration_reform — the bill contains no pathway, status or adjudication provision in either direction; border_wall / lands_energy and the fentanyl keys — nothing in the text touches barriers, land or controlled substances, despite the 15-year enhancement for prior drug misdemeanours being about the offender's record and not about trafficking policy.

issues.rationale: The bill's entire substance is sentence length. Section 2 raises the improper-entry maximum under 8 U.S.C. 1325 from 2 to 5 years and adds a 5-year mandatory minimum, up to life, for a person who entered unlawfully and is later convicted of any crime punishable by more than a year. Section 3 rewrites the reentry penalties of 8 U.S.C. 1326 with a 10-year general maximum, 15 years after three or more drug or person-crime misdemeanours, a non-concurrent 10 years after removal on terrorism grounds, and a 10-year mandatory minimum after an aggravated-felony or any-felony conviction. The tough_on_crime chip reads "crack down on crime with strong policing and tougher sentences for offenders"; a yea is a vote for tougher sentences, which is the chip's own text.

Illegal entry and reentry are the two federal offences the immigration-enforcement system rests on, and this bill raises the penalty for both — the axis the border_security chip labels 'Strong Border & Enforcement'. Coded secondary at 65 rather than primary because the bill adds no barrier, no agent, no detention bed and no removal authority: it is enforcement severity, not enforcement capacity. The related deportations key is declined outright for the same reason.
